content:
Formalization of quantum field theory (QFT) is notoriously hard, as UV divergence is common, meaning that renormalization (and the concept of effective theories) has to be a part of the theory, if we want to be able to map the formal power series to concrete numbers.

A possibly easier target of formalization, which currently appears to have avoided the attention of mathematicians, is condensed matter field theory, also known as many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) in the context of first-principles calculations. Because MBPT is essentially QED with the photo degrees of freedom integrated out in the non-relativistic limit, it has a couple features that set it apart from QFT in high energy physics:

  • The free propagators are not Lorentz covariant,
  • The interaction vertex is the spontaneous four-legged Coulomb vertex, and
  • The interactively corrected single- or mult-electron Green's functions are the product of the theory: there's no LSZ reduction and there's no amplitude.

Despite looking uglier (for high energy physicists), MBPT is more tame in two aspects.

  • The most important point is perhaps it has no UV divergence, as it's always carried out in a lattice system, and the (crystal) momentum has a natural cutoff (i.e. first Brillouin zone boundaries): the missing degrees of freedom translate to band indices.
  • The Fock space is much simpler in MBPT: there's no creation and annihilation of electrons, and there is no Lorentz covariance constraint. Explicitly constructing the many-body Fock space and the many-body Hamiltonian may be witihn the reach, which makes proving the correctness of the Feynman diagrammatic method much easier (like showing that the fully diagrammatically corrected Green's function is indeed the Green's function derived from exact diagonalization) compared with the case of relativistic QFT.

One thing that needs to be done in formalization of MBPT is that we perhaps need another version of FieldOp (https://jstoobysmith.github.io/PhyslibVerso/Physlib/QFT/PerturbationTheory/FeynmanDiagrams/Basic/), which carries a position or a momentum index with it: MBPT is applied to molecules too, which are not periodic and have no momentum-like good quantum numbers.

From the perspective of a physicist there may still be fundamentally hard mathematical problems blocking a formalization. The most important one is perhaps phase transition, where we can naively swap integrals and summations and order of terms in the Feynman diagram series.

Such a formalization, if possible, will also be a solid step towards formalization of e.g. Keldysh field theory.
